Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 32
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.
Password found in configuration file

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

Restricted configurations found
 Potential 2
FilePosition

src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 2

Explanation

The application uses restricted configurations for Azure Container Apps.
These properties can be automatically injected into your application environment by Azure Container Apps to access managed Config Server and managed Eureka Server.
Please remove them from your application, including configuration files, config server files, command line parameters, Java system attributes, and environment variables.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

The application is using a Spring Boot version that has reached its End of OSS Support.
With the officially supported new versions from Spring, you can get the best experience. Here are some steps you can take to update your application to the latest version of Spring Boot:

  • Choose a supported Spring Boot version: Check out Spring Boot Support Versions and determine the most suitable supported Spring Boot version.
  • Update Spring Boot version: Update the Spring Boot version of your application. There are automated tools like Rewrite to help you with the migration.
  • Address code compatibility: Review your application's codebase for any potential compatibility issues with the target Spring Boot version. Update deprecated APIs or features, address any language or library changes, and ensure that your code follows best practices and standards.
  • Test thoroughly: Execute a comprehensive testing process to verify the compatibility and functionality of your application with the new Spring Boot version. Perform unit tests, integration tests, and system tests to validate that all components and dependencies work as expected.

Architecture Diagram

Photo Album is a single-module Java web application for uploading, browsing, viewing, and deleting photos. This read-only assessment describes the checked-in application and Docker Compose topology; it does not establish a running deployment, and no credential values are reproduced.

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle is the application's runtime datastore. The Photo JPA entity maps metadata and a photo_data BLOB to photos; PhotoServiceImpl saves uploaded bytes directly in the database, and the photo-serving endpoint reads those bytes back. Filename and /uploads/ path fields remain compatibility metadata, not an active filesystem upload store; the repository also contains a static sample image. Compose persists Oracle files in oracle_data, mounts oracle-init initialization scripts, and starts the application after the database health check passes. Both application property profiles configure Hibernate ddl-auto=create, so persistent database files do not imply that application tables survive startup unchanged. Database and administrator credentials are externally configured; values are intentionally omitted.

The browser downloads Bootstrap assets from jsDelivr. No application-side cache, message broker, object-storage integration, or remote business API was identified in the main sources. H2 is declared for tests only, not as runtime storage.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • A layered monolith uses constructor injection: MVC controllers depend on PhotoService, whose transactional implementation delegates persistence to PhotoRepository. Thymeleaf serves pages while the same application exposes JSON upload responses and binary images.
  • Photo binaries and metadata share Oracle storage. Spring Data CRUD is combined with Oracle-specific native SQL for ordering and navigation; additional repository queries use Oracle pagination, date formatting, and analytical functions.
  • Gallery and image reads are public; upload and delete POST routes require HTTP Basic authentication. Security is configured as stateless with CSRF disabled, an in-memory administrator, and BCrypt password encoding.

API & Service Communication Contracts

Five explicit HTTP endpoints provide gallery/detail HTML, multipart upload with JSON results, photo bytes, and deletion. Requests use synchronous controller/service calls and database access; browser uploads use asynchronous JavaScript without server-side messaging.

API Endpoints Inventory

All five routes belong to photoalbum-java-app; no URL, header, or query-based API versioning is implemented.

ServiceMethodPathRequest TypeResponse Type
photoalbum-java-app / HomeController.indexGET/No body or declared parameters200 HTML (index view); model contains List and a cache-busting timestamp. Retrieval exceptions produce an empty gallery rather than an error status.
photoalbum-java-app / HomeController.uploadPhotosPOST/uploadHTTP Basic authentication; multipart/form-data with repeated required files parts bound to List200 JSON Map containing success, uploadedPhotos, and failedUploads; includes partial-success and all-file-failure outcomes. 400 JSON for an empty list reaching the handler (success, error); a missing required part is rejected by Spring binding with 400, not necessarily that JSON shape. 401 without valid credentials.
photoalbum-java-app / DetailController.detailGET/detail/{id}Path id: String200 HTML (detail view) with Photo and optional previous/next navigation IDs. 302 redirect to / for missing photo, blank ID reaching the handler, or retrieval exception.
photoalbum-java-app / DetailController.deletePhotoPOST/detail/{id}/deleteHTTP Basic authentication; path id: String; no body required302 redirect to / for success, missing photo, or caught deletion error; flash attributes carry a success/error message, not a JSON response. 401 without valid credentials.
photoalbum-java-app / PhotoFileController.servePhotoGET/photo/{id}Path id: String; browser may append _t for cache busting, but the handler does not bind it200 ResponseEntity with ByteArrayResource image bytes and the stored MIME type. 404 for missing photo/data or blank ID reaching the handler; 500 with no body for caught exceptions.

Photo-byte responses set Cache-Control: no-cache, no-store, must-revalidate, private, Pragma: no-cache, Expires: 0, and X-Photo-ID, X-Photo-Name, X-Photo-Size metadata headers. The compatibility path returned in upload metadata is not the serving endpoint: consumers use /photo/{id}.

Per-file validation/read/save failures normally appear in the HTTP 200 upload failure array rather than as per-file HTTP errors. Unhandled lookup or transaction failures can still propagate as server errors; there is no custom global error contract. Framework multipart-size/binding failures occur before the handler and have no application-defined response schema. Detailed validation belongs in business-workflows.md.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/{HomeController,DetailController,PhotoFileController}.java, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java, src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js.

Communication Patterns

  • Synchronous: Browser HTTP requests enter Spring MVC controllers, which directly call PhotoService/PhotoServiceImpl, then PhotoRepository via JPA/JDBC. Upload parts are processed sequentially; each successful service result triggers a separate lookup to compose response metadata. Detail rendering combines a photo lookup and older/newer navigation lookups within the same service; this is not gateway aggregation.
  • Asynchronous: upload.js uses fetch and FormData to avoid blocking the browser UI. No server-side asynchronous jobs, message brokers, pub/sub, or event-consumer contracts were found.
  • Resilience and timeouts: No application-defined circuit breaker, retry/backoff policy, bulkhead, HTTP client timeout, or JDBC/query timeout was found; no explicit numeric request timeout can be reported. Compose's application restart-on-failure is a process policy, not a request retry. Upload errors are usually represented as per-file results; gallery failures render an empty list, detail failures redirect, deletion failures redirect with flash messages, and binary read failures return 404/500. There is no downstream-service fallback or multi-service response composition.
  • Discovery, routing, balancing: No REST client, gateway, discovery registration, or client-side load balancer was found. Database access uses a configured JDBC address whose default/Compose host is oracle-db, resolved through Compose networking; this is not application service discovery.
  • API availability: Compose starts the application after database health is established. Database connectivity and externally supplied admin credentials are required for normal application startup. Full dependency/readiness and configuration details belong in configuration-inventory.md.
  • Authentication/authorization: Stateless HTTP Basic protects POST /upload and POST /detail/*/delete; unauthenticated requests are challenged with 401. The configured in-memory user has an ADMIN role, but matchers require only authentication, not an explicit role check. Gallery, detail, binary reads, and all other requests are permitted without authentication. No JWT/OAuth2 or method-level authorization was found. CSRF protection is explicitly disabled.
  • Transport: Repository configuration exposes HTTP, with no application TLS listener, forced HTTPS rule, or TLS-terminating proxy definition found. External deployment TLS cannot be inferred. Credential values are intentionally omitted from this report.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java, controller sources, src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java, docker-compose.yml, src/main/resources/application*.properties, src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js.

Resolution chain: Compose resolves ${...} from its invocation environment/local .env before creating containers. The application receives only declared container environment entries; Spring does not itself load the root .env file. Spring then resolves its property sources: command-line arguments, JVM system properties and operating-system environment can override packaged property files; active-profile files override base settings. Environment names such as APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD map to app.admin.password through Spring environment resolution. The datasource placeholders explicitly reference SPRING_DATASOURCE_*.

Startup Dependency Chain

  1. Compose invocation → required environment inputs: interpolation requires nonempty ORACLE_PASSWORD, APP_USER_PASSWORD and APP_ADMIN_PASSWORD before service creation (docker-compose.yml:7,9,36).
  2. Oracle container → database initialization: database files use oracle_data; ./oracle-init is mounted into /container-entrypoint-initdb.d. Image environment provisions the application account; SQL files grant/verify access. create-user.sh has required environment checks and a fixed 30-second sleep before its SQL connection, not a polling retry (oracle-init/create-user.sh:9-22).
  3. Application container → waits for → healthy Oracle container: Compose depends_on.oracle-db.condition=service_healthy. The actual configured health command is image-provided healthcheck.sh, interval 30 seconds, timeout 10 seconds, 15 retries and start period 180 seconds (docker-compose.yml:17-22,39-41). The separate oracle-init/healthcheck.sql is not the command configured in Compose.
  4. Spring application → required datasource/admin properties and database: the password placeholders have no application fallback. No application healthcheck, readiness probe, startup timeout, explicit connection retry policy or config/discovery-server dependency is configured. Compose restart-on-failure applies after process failure, not as an application readiness probe.
  5. Azure setup script, separate provisioning path: Azure account context → resource group → ACR → two-node AKS → ACR attachment → PostgreSQL server/database → firewall rules → FQDN lookup → fixed 30-second wait → database account/grants → .env output (azure-setup.ps1:45-299). This is infrastructure ordering, not evidence that the application has been deployed or migrated.

Secrets Provisioning Workflow

  • Local/Compose: operator copies .env.example to git-ignored .env and replaces placeholder credentials → Compose interpolates required inputs → Oracle receives administrative/application credentials → Java receives datasource credentials and administrator credentials. The application password has no packaged fallback. Oracle SQL initialization grants schema-scoped privileges; the SQL file uses a fixed schema identifier even though APP_USER is configurable.
  • Application access model: the datasource uses database credentials; the administrator is held in an InMemoryUserDetailsManager with BCrypt password encoding (SecurityConfig.java:28-42). No external identity provider or secret-store client is configured.
  • Azure setup: existing Azure CLI account context authenticates provisioning. POSTGRES_ADMIN_PASSWORD and POSTGRES_APP_PASSWORD come from the process environment when provided, otherwise from the script's System.Security.Cryptography.RandomNumberGenerator helper. Administrator credentials create the PostgreSQL application account and grants; application credentials are exported and persisted in .env. ACR admin access is enabled and AKS is attached to ACR. No explicit application managed identity, service-principal configuration, Key Vault policy or application-specific RBAC binding is declared.
  • Repository automation: GitHub-provided/action secret references are consumed by repository workflows, not by an Azure application deployment workflow. No application secret publication to Kubernetes or cloud secret stores was found.
  • Storage/encryption boundary: .env is ignored, but there is no repository-defined encryption-at-rest workflow, Jasypt, sealed secrets, DPAPI or vault integration. BCrypt protects the in-memory administrator representation; it does not encrypt source environment files.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets visitors browse a shared photo collection, inspect individual images, and navigate between uploads. Authenticated users can add multiple photos and permanently remove photos from the collection.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhoto Album / Photo ManagementAn uploaded image together with the descriptive information needed to display and manage it; the sole persisted business entity and practical aggregate boundary.Its image content and metadata form one managed item. Chronological neighbors are derived from other photos, not explicit relationships.
UploadResultPhoto Album / Upload ProcessingA transient per-file operation outcome, not a persisted entity or aggregate. Carries success or failure information for user feedback.Refers to the created Photo on success; the controller combines multiple outcomes into a batch response.

There are no modeled Album, User, ownership, tagging, or sharing-permission entities. The collection is shared rather than partitioned into user-owned albums.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/Photo.java:19-108; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/model/UploadResult.java:6-29.

Service-to-Domain Mapping

This is one application and one business context, not a set of independently deployed domain services. The rows below describe internal responsibilities, not separate microservices.

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
PhotoService / PhotoServiceImplPhoto Management: ingest, retrieve, navigate, deletePhoto; creates transient UploadResult outcomesPhotoRepository and the photo database; local image-header inspection
HomeControllerCollection browsing and batch-upload orchestrationNone; composes Photo summaries and upload outcomesInternal PhotoService
DetailControllerSingle-photo viewing, chronological navigation, removalNone; composes a Photo with neighboring identifiersInternal PhotoService
PhotoFileControllerImage deliveryNone; reads Photo contentInternal PhotoService

PhotoService is the application authority for photo operations; the database is the durable source of truth for both image content and metadata. There are no cross-context entity references, remote domain-service calls, message exchanges, or gateway aggregation.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:28-47; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:24-32; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:19-27; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:24-32.

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload a batch and publish accepted photos

  1. A user selects or drops files on the gallery page. Browser-side Upload admissibility checks filter files before submission; accepted files are sent together to POST /upload.
  2. The security filter requires authentication before upload processing. HomeController applies Batch admission, then calls PhotoService once per submitted file, sequentially.
  3. PhotoService applies Upload admissibility and Image inspection. Rejected files return an unsuccessful UploadResult; processing can continue with other files.
  4. For an accepted file, the service generates a compatibility filename/path, reads image bytes, and extracts dimensions when possible. It creates a Photo and saves content and metadata together.
  5. The controller re-fetches each successful Photo by its returned identifier and projects its display metadata into the successful-results list. Failed outcomes are collected separately.
  6. The response reports Batch outcome. The browser inserts successful photos into the gallery, shows their count, and displays per-file failures. No full-page reload is needed.

This is controller orchestration within one application, not cross-service choreography. Transaction boundaries make the batch a set of individual file operations rather than one all-or-nothing upload.

Evidence: src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:48-132,135-159; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:55-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:81-192; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/config/SecurityConfig.java:46-60.

Workflow 2: Browse the collection and navigate full-size photos

  1. A visitor opens GET /. HomeController retrieves the collection under Chronological ordering, then renders gallery cards.
  2. If collection retrieval fails, the page still renders with an empty photo list. This fallback can look like an empty collection; the controller does not add a distinct database-error message.
  3. Selecting a card enters GET /detail/{id}. DetailController loads the Photo and separately obtains older and newer neighbors under Chronological navigation.
  4. The detail page composes the selected photo with optional neighbor identifiers. Missing neighbors produce no corresponding navigation button; invalid identifiers, absent photos, or lookup failures redirect to the gallery.
  5. Gallery and detail images trigger GET /photo/{id}. PhotoFileController retrieves the stored image bytes and serves them using the photo's recorded media type.
  6. Image availability controls missing-content and retrieval-error outcomes. Browser cache bypassing makes the UI request current image content rather than relying on an old cached image.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-49; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:32-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:37-86; src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:67-87; src/main/resources/static/js/upload.js:176-179.

Workflow 3: Confirm and permanently remove a photo

  1. The detail page presents a browser confirmation before submitting POST /detail/{id}/delete. This is a user-experience safeguard, not a server-side approval state.
  2. Authentication is required. PhotoService looks up the selected Photo and applies Deletion existence.
  3. An existing Photo is removed from the database, including its stored image content; an absent Photo returns a not-found outcome.
  4. DetailController redirects to the gallery with a success, not-found, or failure flash message. There is no soft-delete, recovery, or asynchronous cleanup workflow.

Evidence: src/main/resources/templates/detail.html:50-51; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:64-78; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:198-217.

No scheduled business processes, event-driven consumers, batch jobs, or business-state initialization hooks were found in src/main/java. The application entry point only starts the application. Month filtering, pagination, and statistics queries exist on PhotoRepository but are not invoked by the implemented service/controller workflows; they are not exposed business processes.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/PhotoAlbumApplication.java:9-14; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/repository/PhotoRepository.java:58-100.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no remote business services or gateway joins. The browser communicates with a single application, which reads and writes the shared photo database through PhotoService and PhotoRepository.

  • Upload composition: per-file UploadResult identifies a saved Photo; the controller re-reads that Photo and combines its display metadata with other successes and per-file failures. Image bytes are not included in this upload response; the browser fetches them separately using the photo identifier.
  • Detail composition: the selected Photo supplies its upload timestamp for older/newer lookups. The controller combines the results into a detail view with optional navigation links. These calls are separate service reads, not a single transaction spanning the entire detail response.
  • Content delivery: the same Photo identifier connects gallery/detail metadata to stored image bytes. The generated /uploads/ path is compatibility metadata only; it is not a separate filesystem or object-storage delivery flow.
  • Degradation: collection read failures render an empty gallery; detail lookup/navigation failures redirect home; unavailable image records/content return not found; unexpected image-serving errors return a server error. Upload read failures reject the affected file, while many metadata-inspection problems permit upload without dimensions.
  • Limits of fallback: no circuit breaker, remote-service fallback, retry queue, or compensating action exists. A controller re-fetch failure after a successful upload is not caught inside the batch loop and can interrupt response assembly after earlier files have already been saved.

Evidence: src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java:37-97; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/DetailController.java:38-58; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/PhotoFileController.java:44-86; src/main/java/com/photoalbum/service/impl/PhotoServiceImpl.java:112-185.

Business Workflow Sequence

The primary workflow is authenticated batch upload followed by publication in the shared gallery. Fallback branches below are local business outcomes, not circuit-breaker behavior.

sequenceDiagram actor User as "Photo contributor" participant Browser as "Gallery" participant Access as "Access control" participant Home as "Upload coordinator" participant Service as "Photo management" participant Photo as "Photo aggregate" participant Store as "Photo repository and database" Browser->>Browser: Filter selected files using upload rules User->>Browser: Submit accepted files Browser->>Access: Upload batch alt Not authenticated Access-->>Browser: Authentication required else Authenticated Access->>Home: Process submitted batch loop Each submitted file Home->>Service: Add photo to collection Service->>Service: Check upload rules and inspect image alt Rejected or unreadable file Service-->>Home: File failure with explanation else Accepted file Service->>Photo: Create photo with content and metadata Note over Service,Photo: Some inspection failures allow missing dimensions Service->>Store: Save complete photo alt Save succeeds Store-->>Service: Saved photo Service-->>Home: Successful photo identifier Home->>Service: Retrieve display summary Service->>Store: Look up saved photo Store-->>Service: Photo Service-->>Home: Photo metadata else Save operation reports failure Service-->>Home: File failure with explanation end end end Home-->>Browser: Successful summaries and per-file failures Browser-->>User: Add accepted photos and show feedback end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Upload admissibility: browser checks allow JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP and a maximum size of 10 MiB. The service lowercases the declared MIME type and checks the configured allowlist; it also rejects sizes above the configured limit and empty files. Current application properties set the same allowlist and 10,485,760-byte limit. A missing MIME type results in the generic upload-error path. Declared MIME acceptance is not a guarantee that bytes decode as an image.
  • Batch admission: a null or empty submitted file list returns a bad request. Multipart settings cap individual files at 10 MB and the whole request at 50 MB. A configured maximum of ten files exists, but neither the controller nor browser enforces a file-count rule.
  • Image inspection: when an image reader can determine dimensions, more than 40,000,000 pixels is rejected. An I/O exception during data/header reading fails the file. No reader or a different inspection exception allows processing without dimensions; complete image decoding is not required.
  • Photo validity: original and stored filenames must be nonblank and at most 255 characters; compatibility paths are at most 500 characters; recorded file size must be present and positive; media type must be nonblank and at most 50 characters; upload time must be present. These are declared entity validation constraints, not an explicit controller validation phase.
  • Identity and lifecycle: construction assigns a fresh photo identifier and current upload time; upload independently generates a compatibility filename, preserving the extracted original extension. No duplicate-content/name rejection is implemented. The lifecycle is transient upload → saved/visible Photo → permanently deleted; rejection is an operation outcome, not a persisted status.
  • Batch outcome: response success means at least one saved Photo was re-fetched and included in the successful-results list. Per-file failures may coexist with successes; a nonempty batch with all reported failures still receives a normal response with success false. A successful save whose re-fetch returns empty is omitted from both result lists.
  • Chronological ordering/navigation: initial gallery retrieval orders newest uploads first. Previous selects the closest strictly older upload and next the closest strictly newer upload; equal timestamps are excluded and no secondary tie-break ordering exists. Browser insertion prepends each new card in turn, rather than sorting the entire collection again.
  • Image availability: blank/missing identifiers, absent photos, or absent/empty stored content produce not found. Unexpected serving failures produce a server error. The recorded media type determines delivery format; no thumbnail transformation is performed.
  • Deletion existence: absent photos are a nonexceptional false outcome; existing photos are physically deleted. The collection has no user-ownership relationship to check.

Cross-cutting concerns

  • Transaction boundaries: PhotoServiceImpl is transactional; retrieval and navigation methods are marked read-only. Each file upload is a separate service invocation, and HomeController has no enclosing batch transaction. There is no distributed transaction, saga, or explicit compensation. Upload catches save exceptions and returns an outcome, but deferred flush/commit errors can still escape the service invocation; a reported failure is not a general recovery guarantee.
  • Authorization: reads are public; upload and deletion require an authenticated caller. The configured account has an administrative role, but endpoint rules check authentication rather than explicitly requiring that role. Authentication uses HTTP Basic with stateless sessions; CSRF is disabled. Credentials are externally supplied and are intentionally not reproduced here.
  • Error handling: no custom business exception hierarchy is present. Upload uses UploadResult failures; collection/detail controllers provide the view fallbacks above; deletion maps exceptions to user feedback. No automatic retry or dead-letter mechanism is implemented.
  • Audit/logging: upload acceptance/rejection, retrieval errors, deletion, and image delivery are logged. Image-delivery debug logging includes filenames, identifiers, and a short binary prefix; this is diagnostic logging, not a durable business audit trail. No audit entity or change history is implemented.
  • Computed values and integrity: display dimensions come from image headers when available; UI size/date labels are derived for presentation. Navigation is timestamp-derived. With one standalone Photo entity, there are no bidirectional business associations to maintain.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 2.7.18 is the final 2.7 release and is outside community support; any extended commercial support must be assessed separately. The build targets Java 8 (pom.xml:23–26); moving to Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17 or later and migration from Java EE javax APIs to Jakarta equivalents, particularly relevant to JPA, validation, and security. Commons IO 2.11.0 is an older explicitly pinned release that will not track parent-managed upgrades. Oracle driver compatibility cannot be assessed precisely without its inherited version. This inventory does not establish CVE status.

Notable Observations

  • spring-boot-starter-json is declared explicitly alongside the web starter, which normally includes JSON support transitively; verify redundancy when resolving the dependency tree. Despite its POM comment, this is a JSON starter, not an image-processing library.
  • DevTools is optional but compile-scoped, so it is included in the non-test count. Optionality affects downstream dependency propagation rather than changing its Maven scope.
  • No logging, caching, messaging, or observability libraries are declared directly. Starter-provided transitive libraries are not enumerated or counted because neither their dependency descriptors nor a resolved lockfile are present in the assessed build files.
  • org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-maven-plugin is declared without a version; it inherits parent plugin management and is a build tool, not an application dependency.

No dedicated integration-testing or contract-testing dependency is declared directly. H2 and the runtime Oracle driver represent different database implementations; test fidelity should be evaluated separately, without assuming what tests actually execute from the build declaration alone.

Data Architecture & Persistence Layer

The data layer contains one persistent entity, Photo, mapped to Oracle through Spring Data JPA/Hibernate; H2 is configured for tests. Photo bytes and descriptive metadata reside together in the relational table, rather than in a separate file or object store.

Entity Model

erDiagram %% All persistent entities belong to photo-album. Photo { string id PK "Application-generated UUID; length 36" string originalFileName "Required; length 255" bytes photoData "Nullable LOB" string storedFileName "Required; length 255" string filePath "Nullable compatibility metadata; length 500" Long fileSize "Required; Oracle NUMBER 19 digits" string mimeType "Required; length 50" LocalDateTime uploadedAt "Required; Oracle timestamp" Integer width "Nullable" Integer height "Nullable" }
  • Mapping: Photo maps to photos; camel-case fields have explicit snake-case column names. id is a Java String, photoData is byte[], and the remaining Java types are shown above (string denotes String). There are no foreign keys or entity relationships, so no cardinality edges, bidirectional links, cascade rules, or association fetch settings apply.
  • Keys and indexes: UUID identifiers are assigned in the constructor, not through a database sequence. A nonunique index covers uploaded_at. No additional uniqueness constraints or optimistic-lock version field are declared.
  • Binary loading: photoData is an ordinary @Lob without an explicit lazy-fetch override; custom entity queries select it alongside metadata. There is no separate metadata-only projection for gallery reads.
  • Timestamp: The constructor sets the upload timestamp locally; the mapped Oracle timestamp column also declares a database current-timestamp default. No audit entity or timezone-specific field is declared.
  • Transactions: PhotoServiceImpl has class-level @Transactional; the four read methods override it with read-only transactions. Upload and delete inherit writable transactions.
  • Nonpersistent model: UploadResult is a response DTO, not a table/entity.

Data Ownership Boundaries

One application-owned relational schema contains the discovered domain table. No database-per-service partitioning, shared cross-service tables, remote data aggregation, or cross-service database access was found. H2 is a test substitute, not a second production datastore.

PhotoServiceImpl performs both reads and writes through the same repository/entity model. Read-only transactions do not constitute CQRS: there is no separate read store, event stream, synchronization pipeline, or materialized projection. Photo content is persisted in the row's BLOB; stored filenames and paths are compatibility metadata, not evidence of filesystem persistence. There is no per-user owner key or row-level ownership mapping.
